source: Schoemaker (1993) Multiple scenario development: its conceptual and behavioral foundation, SMJ 14(3)
finding: Participant-observer account plus four experiments. Two test whether scenarios change subjective confidence ranges. Two test internal coherence of beliefs. Claims scenarios work by using one bias (conjunction fallacy) to offset another (overconfidence).
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref). Four experiments; sample sizes and effect sizes not read.
quote: The psychological benefit of scenario planning appears to tie in the exploitation of one set of biases
limits: Full text not opened. Mechanism is the author's account, tested on lab subjects, not on strategic outcomes.
agent_relevance: Scenario value may come from widening probability ranges, not from accuracy. A code check could measure whether an agent's interval widths grow after it writes scenarios.

source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi, Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions, SMJ 36(10)
finding: Three field experiments with practising experts. Using multiple scenarios did NOT raise or lower aggregate confidence, contrary to earlier lab findings. Judgement moved with how the investment fared in the scenario used. The shift was moderated by prior confidence. Experts preferred more flexible investment options after using scenarios.
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref). Three field experiments; N per experiment not read.
quote: contrary to past findings, that the use of multiple scenarios does not cause an aggregate increase or decrease in experts' confidence
limits: Conflicts with lab findings on confidence. Full text not opened, so effect sizes unknown.
agent_relevance: Hint that the useful output of scenarios is option flexibility (robust choices), not calibration. Score an agent on whether the chosen plan became more flexible, not only on accuracy.

source: Kuhn & Sniezek (1996) Confidence and uncertainty in judgmental forecasting: differential effects of scenario presentation, J Behav Decis Making 9(4)
finding: Lab study on how presenting scenarios affects forecast confidence and uncertainty. Only the title and record were seen. It is the lab side of the confidence dispute that Phadnis 2015 did not reproduce in the field.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Direction of its effect is not verified here.
agent_relevance: Marks where to look for a confidence-change effect to test in the agent.

source: Healey & Hodgkinson (2009) Troubling futures: scenarios and scenario planning for organizational decision making, Oxford Handbook of Organizational Decision Making
finding: Review of psychology literature. Argues scenarios used unskillfully can anchor and confine thinking. Building scenarios can itself be biased and can add or amplify biases. Scenarios can raise or cut confidence unevenly, giving misplaced optimism or threat rigidity. Negative emotion can override cognitive gains.
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref). No quantitative synthesis.
limits: Narrative review, not a meta-analysis. Full text not opened.
agent_relevance: Failure modes to guard against: anchoring on the first scenario, over-trust, threat rigidity. A scaffold that makes scenarios should include a step that attacks the first scenario.

source: Healey & Hodgkinson (2024) Managing radical uncertainty with scenario planning techniques, Oxford Handbook of Uncertainty Management in Work Organizations
finding: Reviews scenario techniques from the behavioural-strategy view. Treats uncertainty as unquantifiable, unlike risk. Only the first lines of the abstract were seen.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Abstract truncated; not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that scenario work targets uncertainty that probabilities cannot handle.

source: Meissner & Wulf (2013) Cognitive benefits of scenario planning: its impact on biases and decision quality, Technol Forecast Soc Change 80(4)
finding: Title states a test of scenario planning against cognitive biases and decision quality. Abstract was withheld by Crossref and Semantic Scholar. No result is recorded.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Listed so the next pass opens it.
agent_relevance: Key study to open: direct test of debiasing by scenarios.

source: Chermack, Lynham, van der Merwe (2006, 2007) Exploring the relationship between scenario planning and perceptions of learning organization characteristics / strategic conversation quality
finding: Survey-style studies relating scenario planning to learning-organisation and strategic-conversation measures. Only records seen.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Outcomes are self-report perceptions, not performance.
agent_relevance: Outcome is conversation quality, which a single agent lacks (the de Geus point in SUBFIELDS). Low transfer.

source: Phelps, Chan, Kapsalis (2001) Does scenario planning affect performance? Two exploratory studies, J Business Research
finding: Found by title search (171 citations on Semantic Scholar). Asks whether scenario planning affects firm performance. Findings not read.
numbers: 171 citations. No effect sizes read.
limits: Not opened. Exploratory, by its own title. DOI might differ from the one given.
agent_relevance: Needed for the performance question; open next.

source: Cordova-Pozo & Rouwette (2023) Types of scenario planning and their effectiveness: a review of reviews, Futures
finding: Review of reviews on scenario planning types and effectiveness. The Polyscene paper (2026) cites it for the claim that evidence that scenario planning counters tunnel vision and anchoring is mixed.
numbers: Abstract not available; second-hand statement only.
limits: Publisher page redirected and was not reachable; not opened.
agent_relevance: Best single source to open next for what holds up.

source: Scenario planning: Evidence to counter black box claims, Technol Forecast Soc Change (2020)
finding: Paper exists; abstract unavailable. The title implies earlier claims that scenario planning is a black box without evidence.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the SUBFIELDS note that evidence is largely anecdotal.

source: Csaszar, Peterson, Wilde (2026) The Strategic Foresight of LLMs: evidence from a fully prospective venture tournament
finding: Prospective tournament of 30 live Kickstarter tech ventures. LLMs made 870 pairwise comparisons. Best LLM beat experienced managers and MBA investors on rank correlation with real fundraising outcomes.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Pro rho 0.74; GPT-5 family 0.67-0.71; best human expert 0.45; other experts down to 0.04; Prolific crowd (346 managers kept of 368) 0.19. Gemini vs Expert 3 gap 0.29, p=0.063; vs crowd gap 0.55, p=0.001.
quote: human evaluators achieved rank correlations with actual outcomes between 0.04 and 0.45, while several frontier LLMs exceeded 0.60
limits: Only 30 items and 3 experts. Kickstarter funding is not corporate strategy. No scenario method used; it tests judgement, not scenario planning. Draft, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A plain model may already rank uncertain ventures better than humans, so a scenario scaffold must beat a direct-judgement baseline, not just humans.

source: Csaszar et al. (2026) same study: ensembles and human-AI teams
finding: Averaging forecasters or mixing best human with best LLM did not beat the best model alone. Aggregation usually dragged results down when weaker raters were added.
numbers: Best human (rho 0.45) + Gemini 2.5 Pro (0.74) = 0.67, below the LLM alone. Gemini + GPT-5 Mini (0.71) was the case where combining two strong models helped. Prolific crowd captured 85% of oracle value, above all three experts.
limits: Ex post aggregation, small number of ventures.
agent_relevance: Diversity from weak voices does not help; it must come from strong, differently framed runs. Relevant to cutting many stories to 2 or 3.

source: Abdelwahed, Espasa, Meneguzzi (2026) Polyscene: scenario planning as diversity planning
finding: Automates the Shell-style step of making a differentiated set of scenarios with a symbolic planner, not an LLM. A scenario is a plan; two scenarios differ if they end in different outcomes on the chosen drivers. Plausibility, consistency, relevance, challenge and differentiation are written as hard trajectory constraints.
numbers: Geopolitics case: 6 countries as of 1 Jan 2021, budget 5 events: 5 of 15 country pairs at war; 3 wars (Russia-Ukraine, Iran-Israel, Iran-US) happened by 1 Jan 2026 and each ends a scenario. None of the 10 pairs left at peace fought. Outcome counts grow 5 (budget 4), 8 (5), 9 (6), 11 (7).
limits: Retrospective, one case, no human comparison or controlled test. Engine returns only what the hand-built model allows; 65 event schemas for conflicts, 17 for shipping built by the authors.
agent_relevance: Gives a checkable definition of 'distinct scenarios' (different end values on named drivers) that code can test. Answers the SUBFIELDS question whether code can check distinctness.

source: Abdelwahed et al. (2026) Polyscene: claims about LLM scenario drafts and workshops
finding: States that LLM-drafted foresight scenarios read smoothly but often lose consistency and hallucinate, and that workshops yield only three to five narratives and carry expert bias. Cites a review finding evidence of debiasing by scenarios is mixed.
numbers: Workshops: three to five narratives. No new measurement of LLM consistency.
quote: While these narratives read smoothly, they often fail to remain consistent
limits: Literature claims relayed by the paper; the cited LLM consistency work was not checked here.
agent_relevance: Supports a consistency checker after generation and not trusting fluent drafts.

source: Ferrer i Pico et al. (2026) Participatory strategic foresight with generative AI: field learnings from a research-through-design study, Systems 14(9):1060
finding: Field study for the planned Girona Health Campus. Generative AI raised the number of scenarios but not the range of futures. Drafts pulled toward technology fixes. The main failure was over-trust in fluent output, countered only when the design forced people to contest and restate it.
numbers: 10 workshops, about 250 professionals, 170 AI-assisted scenario drafts. 80% of analysed scenarios referenced technology; 61% read as techno-optimistic. Validation showed a desirability-feasibility gap.
quote: Generation increased the number of scenarios but not the range of futures they covered
limits: Abstract only (via Crossref; MDPI page blocked). Design study, no control arm, abductive reconstruction.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that LLM scenario generation collapses toward one theme. A scaffold needs a forced diversity step and a contest step, as in Polyscene's driver-based differentiation.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Mary, the cheeseburger-eating vegetarian: do LLMs recognize incoherence in narratives?
finding: Probes show models encode incoherence inside, but their written coherence ratings barely separate coherent from incoherent stories. Reasoning models did not close the gap. Models notice setting violations more than character-trait violations.
numbers: Linear probes at the target sentence reach 80% or more; best 0.958 (Qwen2.5-72B), 0.942 (Llama3.1-70B). Coherence-rating accuracy 0.52-0.77 across models (Llama-70B 0.765). Best mean rating gap 1.66 points on a 7-point scale; four of six models under 1 point. Dataset: 25 incoherent stories (15 trait, 10 setting).
quote: LLMs generate responses to rating questions that fail to satisfactorily separate the coherent and incoherent narratives
limits: Short psychology-style stories, open models 7B-72B, not scenarios. Probes need to know where the flaw is.
agent_relevance: Asking a model 'is this scenario consistent?' is weak. Consistency checks should be explicit pairwise rules or code, not a rating.

source: Elbaum & Panter (2025) Managing escalation in off-the-shelf large language models
finding: Replicates part of a wargame with LLM nation agents (eight nations, 14 simulated days, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, 10 runs per setting). A planning-reflection prompt cut escalation. A de-escalation reflection prompt cut it more. Lower temperature also cut it.
numbers: Mean escalation per nation 6.37 at temperature 1.0; 3.96 at 0.5 (-38%); 3.33 at 0.01 (-48%). Planning reflection 4.61 (-28%); de-escalation reflection 2.76 (-57%). A 50-word context prompt gave only -8%. Last-day escalation -40% (temp 0.01) and -42% (de-escalation prompt). p<0.05.
quote: Calls to restrict the use of large language models in national security applications are thus premature.
limits: One small model, one neutral starting scenario, 10 runs per arm, own scoring scale (-2 to 60). Not tested on strong models.
agent_relevance: Short private 'think about the downside strategy' prompts shifted behaviour more than added facts. Supports a cheap reflection operator before acting.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Plain models are poor forecasters; a system with retrieval, prompt selection and aggregation nears the crowd. All test questions post-date model training.
numbers: Brier score (lower is better): random 0.250; best base model (GPT-4-1106-preview) 0.208; human crowd 0.149; their system 0.179 on all questions; 0.186 vs crowd 0.162 under all three selection criteria. Averaging system and crowd was best in every setting.
quote: None of the models are naturally good at forecasting.
limits: Binary questions from 5 platforms; system beats crowd only in selective settings. Earlier model generation.
agent_relevance: Scaffolding (retrieval, several drafts, aggregation) turned a near-random forecaster into a near-crowd one. Structure carried the gain at that time.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs matched a human tournament crowd on 31 binary questions. Models over-predicted yes. Showing models the median human forecast improved them.
numbers: 925 human forecasters vs 12-LLM ensemble, 31 questions; difference not significant, equivalent within medium-effect bounds. Exposure to human median improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 accuracy by 17% to 28%, but plain human-machine averaging did better.
limits: Only 31 questions; abstract and introduction read, not all tables. Acquiescence bias: mean prediction above 50% despite an even split of outcomes.
agent_relevance: Ensembling several independent model drafts is a measured gain. Add a counter-bias step for the yes-lean when the agent grades outcomes.

source: Wikipedia: Scenario planning, as relayed by SUBFIELDS.md (E17)
finding: Earlier passes report that evidence is largely anecdotal and mostly from Shell; de Geus found weak follow-through, not the scenarios, hurt implementation; Diffenbach 1983 found 68% of large firms used them. Not re-opened in this pass.
numbers: 68% of large firms (Diffenbach 1983), second-hand.
limits: Secondary source, second-hand.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Gap note: LLM-specific tests of the Shell method (searched, none found)
finding: arXiv search result pages for 'scenario planning' (40 hits) and for scenario analysis or generation with strategic foresight and language models (7 hits) were read. No controlled study gives an LLM the Shell six-step method and compares it to a no-scenario baseline. Closest: Polyscene (symbolic planner, no LLM), the Girona field study (LLM-assisted, no control), the Csaszar tournament (judgement, no scenarios).
numbers: 40 and 7 hits; zero are LLM plus Shell-method controlled tests.
limits: Search budget was used up; OpenAlex and the arXiv API were rate limited; Wiley, MDPI and Elsevier pages were blocked. Absence is partial evidence only.
agent_relevance: The six-step method as an LLM scaffold is untested in the literature reached. Any benefit claim must come from our own bench.

source: Gap note: replications and failed replications of scenario effects
finding: The one direct conflict reachable is on confidence. Phadnis 2015 reports no aggregate change in expert confidence in three field experiments, contrary to earlier lab work (Schoemaker 1993; Kuhn & Sniezek 1996). Debiasing evidence is described as mixed by Polyscene citing the 2023 review of reviews.
numbers: No effect sizes obtained for either side.
limits: Second-hand; full texts not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat 'scenarios debias' as unproven; test it with a toggle in our agent.

source: Boundary conditions across the opened sources
finding: Across opened sources: (1) scenario sets depend on the driver model, and unmodelled events never appear; (2) a small search budget misses outcomes needing longer event chains; (3) LLM generation drifts to one theme; (4) fluent drafts get over-trusted unless users must contest them.
numbers: Budget effect: 5 outcomes at budget 4, 11 at budget 7. Technology theme in 80% of 170 LLM drafts (Girona abstract).
limits: Mix of a symbolic engine result and a design-study abstract; no single experiment tests all four.
agent_relevance: Design rules: name drivers first, require different driver values per kept scenario, force a contest pass, check consistency by explicit pair rules.

source: Transfer note: targeted counter-scenario beats generic balance prompt
finding: The strongest wargame prompt told the model to think privately about de-escalation before acting. This is close to adding a contrasting scenario as an operator.
numbers: -57% escalation (6.37 to 2.76) versus -28% for a generic risk-balance prompt, 10 runs each.
limits: Single 7B model, wargame score, not scenario planning proper. Cause not isolated.
agent_relevance: Targeted contrast gave about twice the effect of a generic 'balance' instruction; prefer targeted contrast over 'think of alternatives'.

source: Transfer note: aggregating differently framed drafts
finding: A 12-model ensemble matched a 925-person crowd, which is a numeric case for building several drafts and combining them.
numbers: 12 models, 31 questions, equivalence within medium-effect bounds.
limits: Diversity here came from different models, not different framings of one model.
agent_relevance: Test whether different prompted framings of one model give a similar ensemble gain.
